implementation_notes: Ruby ships the whole structure in the standard library: include Singleton makes new and allocate private, defines Klass.instance (created lazily on first call under a Mutex), preserves the property across inheritance and clone, raises TypeError on clone/dup, and routes Marshal through _dump/_load so deserialisation returns the same object. The mixin is worth it when the singleton is a class instance with its own initialisation; when it is really a namespace, idiomatic Ruby prefers a module (module_function or extend self) or a frozen constant, because a module already is a single object.
code_sketch:
require 'singleton'

class Config
  include Singleton

  def initialize
    @theme = ENV.fetch('THEME', 'light')
  end
end

Config.instance   #=> the same object on every call
# Config.new      #=> NoMethodError: new is private
pitfalls: One instance per process - and, because the stdlib installs a Ractor-local variant when Ractors are available, one per Ractor as well: Config.instance inside a Ractor is not the main Ractor's object.
fork inherits the parent's instance without re-running initialize, so a connection or lock held by the singleton is shared with the child process.
Marshal round trips only return the same instance through the default _load; a class that overrides _load or _dump incorrectly can resurrect a second object or lose state.
The mutex guards creation, not use: unsynchronised mutation of the instance's state is still a data race.
